original_question: Let G be a graph, let P be a graph property, and call a matching M of G a P-matching when the induced subgraph <M> has property P. For each P-matching family introduced in the survey, develop characterization theorems that determine exactly when a given matching M is a maximum P-matching, rather than merely a maximal one.
target_in_paper: Nearest paper-faithful target: the survey's open-problem direction of characterizing, for each surveyed P-matching notion, the graphs G on which maximal P-matchings are automatically maximum P-matchings; in the paper's standard notation, this is the graph-level condition beta_P^-(G) = beta_P(G), not a certification problem for a single fixed matching M.
correct_elements: Your draft correctly uses the paper's P-matching paradigm: a matching is filtered by a graph property P of the induced subgraph on its saturated vertices, and the real issue is the gap between maximal and maximum P-matchings. It also correctly asks for characterizations rather than ad hoc examples.
missing_details: The paper-faithful formulation is graph-level, not matching-level: it asks to characterize graphs G for which every maximal P-matching is maximum, rather than to characterize when a particular matching M is maximum.
You need the paper's notation G[M] for the induced subgraph on the vertices incident with the edges of M.
You need the upper parameter beta_P(G), the maximum cardinality of a P-matching.
You need the lower parameter beta_P^-(G), the minimum cardinality of a maximal P-matching.
The key stand-alone criterion is beta_P^-(G) = beta_P(G), equivalently that all maximal P-matchings have the same size.
The specific P-families should be those actually surveyed under the P-matching framework, not an unspecified open-ended class of graph properties.
A fully stand-alone question should respect family-specific conventions from the survey/framework, e.g. the special |M| = 1 conventions for disconnected and isolate-free matchings.
The ambient setting should be finite simple graphs, which is the default context of the survey literature summarized here.

If the question is meant to range over the canonical surveyed families, those definitions must be fixed explicitly: ordinary, induced/strong, uniquely restricted, connected, isolate-free, acyclic, and disconnected matchings (as defined in the P-matching framework).
refined_question: For each P-matching notion actually treated in the survey's P-matching framework—namely, for each specified property P defining a matching M by the condition that the induced subgraph G[M] on the vertices saturated by M has property P—characterize the finite simple graphs G for which every maximal P-matching is a maximum P-matching; equivalently, determine exactly those graphs G satisfying beta_P^-(G) = beta_P(G), where beta_P(G) is the maximum size of a P-matching in G and beta_P^-(G) is the minimum size of a maximal P-matching.
equivalent_formulation: For each surveyed P-matching family, characterize the finite simple graphs G in which all maximal P-matchings have the same cardinality.
justification: The draft is not fully paper-faithful because it shifts from the natural graph-level problem in this literature to a certification problem for a fixed matching M. In the standard P-matching setup, one defines G[M], beta_P(G), and beta_P^-(G), and the maximal-versus-maximum question is expressed as the equality beta_P^-(G) = beta_P(G). That is exactly the form in which analogous notions are studied for ordinary matchings (equimatchable graphs) and induced matchings (well-indumatched graphs). The 2018 paper is a brief survey of such matching varieties; however, the accessible arXiv rendering exposed only the abstract/metadata, so the refined question is reconstructed from the foundational P-matching definitions and the immediately adjacent maximal-versus-maximum literature that the survey is summarizing.
